extracted.intended_audience: writers looking for online critique groups or critique partners
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and evaluating online critique circles and workshops to get feedback on creative writing (stories, novels, poetry, queries). The page lists platforms, communities, and the features that make them suitable for different writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feedback quality (constructive/actionable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feedback should be substantive, actionable, and framed constructively rather than ‘scorched earth’ or merely congratulatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page repeatedly emphasizes that high-quality groups deliver thorough, constructive criticism (described with words like “insightful,” “thorough,” “constructive,” “actionable,” or “gimlet‑eyed”). It warns feedback quality can vary (e.g., newer members may give weaker critiques) and highlights communities that train reviewers or use metacritique to keep standards high (Critters, Prolitfic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocity systems (give-to-get rules: credits/karma/points)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many communities require or incentivize giving critiques in order to receive them, using explicit exchange systems such as credits, karma, or points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Critique Circle uses credits earned by offering reviews (every 3 reviews = a posting credit); Scribophile uses karma points; The Next Big Writer uses a points system to guarantee substantive feedback. These systems regulate throughput and encourage reviewers to contribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guaranteed number/level of critiques
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the platform promises a minimum number or quality of critiques per submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scribophile promises 3 insightful critiques per submission; Critters aims for 15–20 thoughtful responses per piece; some sites (FaithWriters) guarantee feedback by occasionally hiring pro editors. Check each site's stated guarantees before relying on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership cost and payment model
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the group is free, has paid tiers, subscription pricing, or pay-for-feedback options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page lists pricing models and trial offers (e.g., Inked Voices $10/month or $75/year after a trial; NovelPro $120/year; The Next Big Writer subscription tiers; Writing.Com paid tiers; paid editorial evaluations on YeahWrite). Some allow paying to receive feedback or skip participation requirements (FaithWriters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership selectiveness / admission requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: If entry is open or selective, including required sample submissions or application exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NovelPro requires finished-manuscript samples and a critique exercise; The Desk Drawer requires a 100–250-word writing sample for membership; some groups are invite-only or curated, which raises average critique quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission limits (word counts, number per month)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules that cap how much you can submit (per item length or monthly quotas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: FaithWriters limits submissions to 1,000 words and 4 per month; Online Writing Workshop limits submissions to 7,000 words; Scribophile free membership allows two 3,000-word pieces; many groups impose chapter- or excerpt-based limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation/commitment requirements to remain in good standing
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimum activity expected (e.g., number of critiques per submission or per period).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical rules: The Desk Drawer requires 3 posts a month (1 SUB + 2 CRITS or 3 CRITS); Critters expects ~1 critique/week; Poetry Free-for-All and others require 3 reviews per submitted piece; Writing to Publish requires two critiques before submitting. Failure to meet requirements can restrict posting privileges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation, community rules, and civility enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Level and strictness of moderation: bans on self-promotion, forbidding harsh critiques, content rules (PG-13), and how moderators intervene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several groups ban self-promotion and scorched-earth critiques (Beta Readers and Critique Partners, Fiction Writing group). Admin/mod involvement (e.g., Writers World founder participating) is highlighted as a sign of quality. Some groups enforce age/content rules (18+), and tone rules (be kind).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer expertise and professional involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of industry professionals (agents, editors, publishers) or experienced mentors who provide feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sites note agent/publisher lurkers (YouWriteOn, Online Writing Workshop), paid pro critiques (Christopher Fielden team, YeahWrite editorial evaluations), and podcasts/reviews by agents (Litopia’s Pop-Up Submissions). Professional involvement can increase chance of discovery and higher-calibre feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform/tooling and UX features
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical features that affect workflow: version control, multimedia support, calendar notifications, analytics, graphs, or Google‑Docs style collaboration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique It supports audio/video feedback; Inked Voices has version control and calendar notifications; WritersCafe provides graphs/analytics. These tools help coordination, revision tracking, and reviewer variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre focus and specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the group is generalist or specialized by genre (poetry, YA, romance, sci‑fi, historical, Christian, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page groups general critique communities separately from genre-specific ones and lists many niche groups (Critters/online workshops for SFF/Horror, Romance Critters, FaithWriters, Historical Novel Society groups). Genre focus affects reviewer expertise and expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop structure and cadence (prompts, SUB/CRIT systems, live chat)
rubrics_metrics.description: How the group organizes workshopping: scheduled prompts, SUB/CRIT exchange systems, live meetings, or open forums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Desk Drawer uses weekly prompts and SUB/CRIT protocol; 10 Minute Novelists runs weekly #BuddyDay threads; Writing to Publish meets live in chat every other Monday; some run weekly contests or challenges (YeahWrite, Reedsy Prompts). Structure influences feedback regularity and writer discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turnaround speed and queue systems
rubrics_metrics.description: How quickly submissions are routed for review and whether there are queues or expedited tracks for newbies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique Circle places new users in a Newbie Queue to accelerate feedback; NovelPro’s application critique has a 2-day turnaround. Queue and turnaround policies affect how fast you get actionable responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer reputation, weighting and metacritique
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether review influence is weighted by reviewer reputation/engagement, and whether feedback itself is rated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prolitfic weights reviews by ‘Spark’ (site engagement); Scribophile uses reactions to rate critiques; Prolitfic practices metacritique (reviewing critiques to maintain quality). Weighting helps surface higher-quality reviews in aggregate ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit rating rubrics / evaluation categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal category-based rating systems that break critique into measurable dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: YouWriteOn uses star ratings in eight categories: characters, story, pace and structure, use of language, narrative voice, dialogue, settings, and themes and ideas. Prolitfic uses a 5‑star rating rubric. Such rubrics standardize feedback across reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentives beyond critique (contests, prizes, publication pathways)
rubrics_metrics.description: Opportunities to win contests, earn cash prizes, or be discovered/published via the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reedsy Prompts offers cash prizes and encourages reciprocal critique; Next Big Writer runs contests with cash and professional critiques; SwoonReads is tied to a Macmillan imprint with potential publication and a $10,000 advance. Contests can motivate participation and visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types/levels of editorial feedback offered (line edit, developmental, beta read)
rubrics_metrics.description: Availability of different depths of editorial service: casual reader feedback, developmental edits, line edits, or in-depth beta reads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: YeahWrite offers paid developmental edits or line edits; Romance Critters offers in-depth beta reads after ten full critiques; some platforms (Christopher Fielden, Reedsy marketplace) offer paid editorial assessments. Know whether you need a developmental critique or surface-level notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy, group size, and invite-only policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether workshops are private/invite-only and how group size caps may affect intimacy and attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inked Voices workshops are private and capped at 8 members; NovelPro caps membership at 50. Smaller, invite-only groups often yield more intimate, higher-effort critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training and culture around learning to critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the community teaches critique skills, emphasizes critique-as-craft, or encourages metacritique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critters treats critique as a craft and expects members to learn to read with empathy and acumen; Prolitfic encourages metacritique; Writer’s Digest aggregates critique guidelines to help members give and receive better feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age and content restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Limits on member age or content allowed in the group (e.g., 18+, PG‑13, no erotica).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some groups have age or content rules: Hatrack River is 18+, Fantasy & Science Fiction Writers in America requires PG‑13 content, Fiction Writers Global steers erotica writers elsewhere. These rules shape what material you can post.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching services and partner-finding features
rubrics_metrics.description: Tools or boards that help writers find compatible critique partners by experience, genre, or goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Writers Match functions like matchmaking by experience/genre; WFWA and Sub It Club run Critique Partner Matchup services. Matching reduces friction when seeking long-term beta partners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guarantees or limits on feedback frequency/availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules about how often members can receive critiques or how many pieces are accepted in a given period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FaithWriters limits members to 4 submissions/month; Writing.Com free portfolio limits the number of items stored; some groups impose monthly quotas to ensure equitable reviewer attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community tone: supportive vs gimlet‑eyed/harsh
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the group emphasizes encouragement and low-stakes practice or gimlet‑eyed, publishable-level critique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ABCTales and My Writers Circle are described as wholesome/encouraging and low-stakes; Eratosphere and Critters are described as intense, high-standards workshops better suited to experienced writers. Choose based on how you handle blunt feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery and agent/publisher exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Likelihood that agents, publishers, or Big Five reps will see work posted and provide professional attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: YouWriteOn and Online Writing Workshop note agent/publisher presence; Litopia’s Pop-Up Submissions features agent reviews; SwoonReads is directly connected to Macmillan. Presence of industry eyes can be a draw for writers seeking publication opportunities.
